name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,305

indicators.note: sent back, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: a pal is a mate
the possessive S comes along

annotation.surface: A friend comes home and puts their make-up on.
annotation.walkthrough: SLAP is informal British slang for make-up, especially heavy stage paint; the surface wants you to read 'make-up' as someone's character.
annotation.definitionFit: Slap is theatrical and informal British slang for cosmetics.

indicators.note: the soldiers burst apart and land in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder
E = energy, the physics symbol, joined to the fodder

annotation.surface: Old soldiers charging about full of pep.
annotation.walkthrough: Tommies are British private soldiers (from Tommy Atkins). 'Former' looks like it describes the tommies, but it is the definition: 'sometime' as an adjective means one-time.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: as an adjective, sometime means one-time or erstwhile, describing what someone used to be.

entries.clue: Incendiary crime of vicar after power cut (5)

indicators.note: the P is cut off the front of the word

blocks.note: a parson is a vicar
P = power, the physics symbol; this is what is removed

annotation.surface: A vicar commits a fire-raising crime after a blackout.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Power cut' reads as a blackout; split it, and power is the P that is cut from PARSON.
annotation.definitionFit: Arson is the crime of deliberately setting fire to property.

blocks.note: S = son, as in genealogies
crammed = packed tight

annotation.surface: A boy stuffed his bag and ran away from home.
annotation.definitionFit: To scram is to leave in a hurry, so scrammed is fled.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Packed' pretends to be about luggage before fleeing; it is the word that follows the S. Scram is informal for clearing off fast.

blocks.note: to carpet someone is to call them in for a telling-off
a weeper is someone crying

annotation.surface: A cleaning lady tells off someone who is crying.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cleaner' looks like a person doing the scolding; it is the push-along gadget. The break falls CARPETS/WEEPER, not at the enumeration's CARPET/SWEEPER.
annotation.definitionFit: A carpet sweeper is a manual device with rotating brushes for cleaning carpets.

entries.clue: Starts to arrange social function in Berkshire town (5)

indicators.note: take the starting letters of the words that follow

blocks.note: first letters of Arrange and Social
cot is short for cotangent, a trigonometric function

annotation.surface: Someone begins organising a party in an English town.
annotation.walkthrough: Ascot, a town in Berkshire, west of London, is home to a famous racecourse. 'Social function' reads as a party, but the two words belong to different pieces: social starts AS, function is the maths sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by location: the racecourse town lies in the English county of Berkshire, west of London.

blocks.note: swallow here is the noun, the bird, and this relative of it is the one wanted
I = one, the Roman numeral

annotation.surface: An instruction to knock back a single drink.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Swallow' reads as a verb about drinking, which fits the cocktail; it is the noun, the bird, and the martin is a close relative.
annotation.definitionFit: A martini is a cocktail of gin or vodka with vermouth.

entries.clue: Twerp from Telford periodically turned up (4)

indicators.note: something that happens periodically recurs at regular intervals, so take letters at a regular step
in a down entry, turned up means the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters: T, L, O, D

annotation.surface: A fool from an English town keeps showing up.
annotation.walkthrough: Telford is a town in Shropshire, England. 'Turned up' pretends to mean arrived; in a down clue it means flipped.
annotation.definitionFit: A twerp and a dolt are both stupid people.

entries.clue: Extremely louche aristocrat allowed to go unpunished (3,3)

indicators.note: take the extremes, the first and last letters

blocks.note: the ends of LouchE
toff is British slang for a posh or upper-class person

annotation.surface: A dissolute nobleman escapes punishment, as the upper class so often do.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' looks like an intensifier for louche; it asks for the outside letters instead.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone let off has been allowed to go without the punishment they faced.

indicators.note: the letters are worked over energetically into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: A therapist puts their arm into the work.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface describes exactly what a masseur does, and 'vigorously' is the kneading that rearranges the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A masseur treats the body by massage, a physical therapy.

indicators.note: a coat is the outside, so take the outer letters

blocks.note: 'My!' and 'Cor!' are both exclamations of surprise
the outside letters of AnimaL

annotation.surface: Someone boasts that their pet has a pink coat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'My' looks like a possessive; it is the exclamation, and COR is its British equivalent. The animal's coat is not fur but its first and last letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Coral is a pinkish-red shade.

blocks.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
go = energy, dash

annotation.surface: A dance performed to the rhythm with plenty of spirit.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beat' reads as the musical pulse of the dance; it is the verb, to thrash.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the Argentine ballroom dance is one example of a dance.

entries.clue: Inevitably result in ear, nose and throat trouble. (6)

blocks.note: ENT is the medical abbreviation for ear, nose and throat
to ail is to trouble or afflict

annotation.surface: A cold that settles in your head and throat leads to further problems.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the front and the rest reads like a symptom list; ENT is the name of the hospital department.
annotation.definitionFit: If one thing entails another, it necessarily brings it about.

indicators.note: reported means spoken, so go by the sound

blocks.note: to nick is British slang for to steal, so nickers are thieves

annotation.surface: Burglars caught stealing underwear are turned in to the police.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reported' looks like the thieves were grassed up; it says the answer sounds like them. Knickers are women's underpants in Britain.
annotation.definitionFit: Knickers are underpants, chiefly women's, in British usage.

indicators.note: the letters are not in their usual order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

annotation.surface: Evidence that an anatomist is remarkably good at the job.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Unusually fine' reads as high praise; 'unusually' is working on both words that follow.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something that makes a thing visible, an outward display of it, is a sign.

blocks.note: in Buddhism, the final release from suffering and the cycle of rebirth
a band here, the Seattle grunge trio fronted by Kurt Cobain

annotation.surface: The final aim of a Buddhist community.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Group' reads as a sangha or religious community; it is the rock band.
annotation.definitionFit: In Buddhism nirvana is the final state of enlightenment, and Nirvana was a famous band.

indicators.note: agitated and confused, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 6 letters

annotation.surface: Someone admits they are nearly lost and getting rattled.
annotation.definitionFit: Almost and practically both mean very nearly.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a flustered traveller; 'Practically' at the front is the definition, meaning nearly.

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the words that follow

blocks.note: seconD ROW SEat

annotation.surface: Nodding off in a seat near the front.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second' wants to give S and 'row' wants to be a piece of a charade; the answer is simply sitting across the words.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean to doze lightly, half asleep.

indicators.note: said means spoken, so go by the sound

blocks.note: the contraction of 'we will', which sounds like the word for a round part of a cart

annotation.surface: Someone announced that they would come round.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Go round' reads as a social visit; it means to turn or rotate.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to wheel is to turn or circle about a point.

entries.clue: On reflection, Channel Islands school is fabulous (5)

indicators.note: as in a mirror, the letters are flipped

blocks.note: CI is the abbreviation for the Channel Islands
a gam is a school of whales

annotation.surface: Thinking it over, a school in Jersey or Guernsey is wonderful.
annotation.walkthrough: The Channel Islands are British Crown dependencies off Normandy, including Jersey and Guernsey. 'School' is not a place of learning but a pod of whales.
annotation.definitionFit: Informal British praise: calling something magic means it is marvellous, fabulous.

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so take the letter at the end of the next word

blocks.note: the last letter of stayinG
rump = behind, the backside

annotation.surface: A sulky person at last agrees to remain after the others leave.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Staying behind' reads as one phrase; the two words split, and 'behind' is the backside.
annotation.definitionFit: A grump is a bad-tempered, surly person.

blocks.note: to overlook something, as in not spotting a typo
a young unmarried woman, as used in the courtesy title

annotation.surface: Someone overlooks a young woman.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: to fail to register something, and the title or term for an unmarried young woman.
annotation.walkthrough: Two plain meanings side by side; the surface reads as someone not noticing a young woman.

entries.clue: Mental picture of one’s later years (5)

blocks.note: one's = one is = I'M, with I as one
age = old age, the later years of life

annotation.surface: How a person imagines their own old age.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One's' reads as a possessive; read it as 'one is', and with I standing for one, 'I am' contracts to I'M.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a picture held in the mind is an image, as in imagination.

entries.clue: Our pets running amok in carriage (7)

indicators.note: the letters run wild into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 7 letters

annotation.surface: The family animals are going wild inside a horse-drawn coach.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Carriage' reads as a vehicle; it is the way you hold your body.
annotation.definitionFit: Carriage and posture both mean the way a person holds themselves.

blocks.note: small = humble, modest
to fry is to cook

annotation.surface: The kids of a cook from a modest background.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Humble cook' reads as a lowly chef; the two words are separate pieces, and 'cook' is a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Small fry is an informal term for young children, as well as unimportant people.

entries.clue: Imitates war poets every so often (4)

blocks.note: the 2nd, 4th, 6th and 8th letters: wAr PoEtS

annotation.surface: Someone copies the style of poets like Owen and Sassoon now and then.
annotation.definitionFit: To ape someone is to imitate them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'War poets' conjures Owen and Sassoon, but it is only a letter source, and 'every so often' takes the even letters.
